Nitin, you've been eating biscuits for dinner since you came to Kolkata, haven't you? I can tell. Let old Raghav tell you what I did in my first month here, twenty years ago, when I didn't know a single soul.
First week: I found a tiffin aunty two lanes away. Rice, dal, one sabzi, every evening at eight. Not fancy. But I knew dinner would come.
Second week: I joined a Sunday morning chess group in the park near Deshapriya. Retired uncles and college students, arguing over every move. I went every Sunday, even when I lost.
Third week: I wrote three numbers on a card in my wallet. The doctor at the corner clinic, the landlord, and the tiffin aunty, because she knew everyone.
In the fourth week I got a fever. The tiffin aunty sent soup, and one of the chess uncles drove me to the doctor. By then the city wasn't strange any more. So, Nitin. Tiffin first. Go.

qa.a: In the park near Deshapriya.

qa.q: How might young Raghav have felt when the fever came in the fourth week?
qa.a: Unwell and a little scared, but relieved and cared for when the tiffin aunty and a chess uncle stepped in.

qa.q: Which step in the story mattered most when the fever came, and why?
qa.a: Building the small network, the tiffin aunty and the chess group, since they sent soup and got Raghav to the doctor.

qa.q: How might the tiffin aunty have seen young Raghav?
qa.a: As a lonely regular she could look out for, which is why soup arrived when Raghav fell ill.

Kishore arrived in Guwahati in June with two bags, a job at a pharma warehouse and not a word of Assamese. The monsoon started the same week. For ten days he ate at a different stall each night, got lost twice, and felt like a visitor.
So he made a list and gave himself a month. Week one: a tiffin service. His colleague Jagdish pointed him to a woman near Zoo Road who sent rice, dal and fish curry for ₹2,800 a month. Week two: a hobby. He found a Saturday football group on a college ground, and played in ankle-deep mud with students who taught him three Assamese words a game. Week three: he saved numbers on his phone and on paper: a clinic doctor near his lane, the landlord, Jagdish.
In week four, when water entered the ground floor of his building, he knew exactly whom to call first. The landlord came with sandbags. The football group came with a spare mattress.

qa.a: ₹2,800 a month.

qa.a: Lost and lonely, like a visitor in a strange city, eating at a different stall every night.

grounding: Shows a newcomer building a tiffin routine, a weekend hobby group and a list of emergency contacts within a month in a strange city.

She sits up until morning with the lights on, and calls her colleague Santosh at seven.
Day 12. Santosh and his wife help her move into a working women's hostel near the office, ₹7,500 a month. She loses the ₹4,000 deposit. She sleeps through the night for the first time in three days.

Nilesh, you're telling me the room is cheap. Very good. Now let your Baljeet bua tell you about the cheapest room I ever took.
My first job was in Delhi, in 1998. I found a room in a lane behind the railway line for four hundred rupees. Everyone else was asking nine hundred. I thought I'd been clever. I saw it once, at two in the afternoon.
At night that lane had no lights at all. The door closed with a bolt you could lift with a hairpin. One night I came home and found my trunk opened, my radio and my savings envelope gone. I didn't sleep there again; I went to my friend Kamla's hostel that same night and told the landlord in the morning.
Four hundred rupees cost me everything I'd saved in three months. So, Nilesh. Before you pay, go back at ten at night. Check the lock with your own hands. Then tell me it's cheap.

qa.q: How much was the room behind the railway line?
qa.a: Four hundred rupees.

qa.q: How did young Baljeet feel after finding the trunk opened?
qa.a: Shaken and unsafe, enough never to sleep there again, and upset at losing three months of savings.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have prevented the loss?
qa.a: Visiting the lane after dark and checking the bolt before paying, instead of seeing the room only at two in the afternoon.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt when young Baljeet arrived at the hostel that night?
qa.a: Probably worried and glad to help, taking in a frightened friend without questions.

When Trisha got a teaching post at a school in Haldwani, a broker offered her a flat near the bus stand on an eleven-month lease. 'Sign today, madam, or it's gone.'
She didn't. She booked two weeks in a small guest house run by a family near the old market, ₹350 a night, and used the time as a test.
By the fourth day she knew the bus-stand flat would have been a mistake: the school was on the other side of town, and the shared jeeps ran full in the mornings. By the tenth day, Wasim, who ran the stationery shop outside the school, had told her which lanes flooded in the rains and which landlords returned deposits.
On day thirteen she signed a lease for a ground-floor room ten minutes' walk from school, ₹4,500 a month, with a landlady Wasim vouched for. The thirteen nights had cost her ₹4,550. She guessed the wrong flat would have cost far more.

qa.q: How much did the guest house cost per night?
qa.a: ₹350 a night.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt on day thirteen, signing the new lease?
qa.a: Relieved and confident, knowing the room fits her real commute and comes with a landlady someone she trusts vouched for.

qa.q: What else could Trisha have tested during the two weeks?
qa.a: The walk home after dark and where she would buy groceries, so the new place fits her whole routine.

Hana arrived in Berlin for her first job with a list of flats she'd found online, all cheaper in Neukölln, all asking for a twelve-month contract. Instead, she rented a room for two weeks from Selin, a student subletting while she visited family in Izmir.
She treated the fortnight like homework. She rode the underground at rush hour to see how long her commute really was: forty-five minutes, with a change. She walked the streets near the listings at night. She asked colleagues where they lived and what they paid.
By the second week she had crossed out two areas. One was too far; one was loud until three every morning. A colleague mentioned a shared flat in Wedding, twenty minutes from work, with a room free next month.
Hana visited it on day twelve and signed on day fourteen, the morning Selin came back. 'You look like you've lived here a year,' Selin said, handing her a key ring as a goodbye.

Jeevan's stomach had been hurting on and off for weeks, mostly after dinner. His flatmate Ojas kept sending him videos: 'Drink this seed water.' 'Stop eating wheat.' 'It's definitely stress.'
On Thursday Jeevan stopped scrolling and booked an appointment with a general physician at a clinic in Jayanagar for Saturday morning.
On Friday night he made a note on his phone. When it started: around the middle of last month. When it's worse: after spicy food, late dinners, and lying down straight after eating. What helps: nothing much. Anything else: waking up at night with it.
At the clinic he read from the note. The doctor asked questions, examined his stomach and said a couple of tests would help. Jeevan asked, 'What are the tests for, and what happens after?' The doctor explained both and wrote them down.
On the way home he muted the video group.

qa.a: After spicy food, late dinners, and lying down straight after eating.

'Headache again?' Usha asked as Ankita came in and dropped onto the sofa.
'Fourth time this week, Maa. Someone at office said it's screen time. Someone online said it's worse than that.'
'And what does a doctor say?'
'I haven't asked one.'
'Then that's the first thing.' Usha picked up her phone. 'Dr Kulkarni at the clinic downstairs has Saturday slots.'

Vikas has made several errors this week and looks exhausted. Today I asked if he was all right. He said he hadn't slept properly in about ten days.
He told me he'd noticed a small swelling under his jaw a few weeks ago. Instead of seeing a doctor, he had been reading health forums every night, sometimes until 3 a.m. Each thread offered a worse explanation than the last, and by now he was convinced it was something very serious. 'I didn't want to go and hear it,' he said. 'So I kept reading instead.'
I told him I couldn't say what it was, and neither could the forums; only a doctor who examined him could. With his agreement, we booked an appointment at the clinic our insurance covers for tomorrow morning, and I've given him the time off to go.
I'll check in with him after the appointment.

Tuesday, 2:40 a.m. Uday's diary.
Can't sleep, so writing instead. The mole on my left arm looks bigger than I remember. Or I think it does. I started reading about it at 11. Three hours, eleven forums. Every page matches something, and every match is worse than the last. One post had photos I wish I hadn't seen.
My heart is thudding. I've checked the arm under the torch maybe twenty times. I haven't told anyone. I keep thinking if I go to a doctor and they say it, then it's real.
It's been like this for five nights now. Skipped the gym, forgot to return Amma's call, nearly missed a deadline.
Naveen heard me moving and knocked. I showed him. He said, 'You've read everything except a doctor's opinion.' He's booking the skin clinic near the office for me in the morning, and he's coming along.
Maybe I'll sleep now. Maybe not.

Dalia's right wrist had ached since spring, when her design studio in Vancouver took on a huge rebrand. Some mornings she couldn't hold her coffee cup without wincing.
Her flatmate Bao noticed her shaking out her hand at dinner. 'Have you seen someone?'
'After the deadline.'
The deadline moved twice. Dalia kept a wrist brace in her bag and a quiet dread in her chest. If a doctor told her to stop drawing, what would she do? Not knowing felt safer than knowing.
Nine weeks later the pain woke her at night. Bao sat with her while she booked a clinic slot for the next morning. The doctor examined her wrist, asked why she had waited so long, and referred her to a physiotherapist, saying recovery would probably take longer now than if she'd come in sooner.
Walking home, Dalia said, 'I was scared of losing my job. I nearly wrecked my wrist for it.'
'Yes,' Bao said. 'Let's not do that again.'

Zeenat's appointment at the district hospital in Bidar was at nine, and the outpatient hall would be full by eight. The night before, she sat on the charpai with her younger brother Arif and a school notebook.
'I always go blank in front of doctors,' she said. 'Write what I ask, and what the doctor says. Exactly.'
Together they wrote her questions. What are these tests for? When will results come? Is there anything to avoid until then? Whom do we call if the pain gets worse before the next visit?
In the morning they waited two hours on a bench. When Dr Sachin Patil finally called her in, Zeenat's hands were shaking, and she forgot the first question completely. Arif read it out for her. He wrote while the doctor explained, and asked for the name of one test to be repeated slowly.
On the bus home, Zeenat read his notes twice. 'I only remember half of this,' she said. 'Good thing you remember the other half.'

Before locking up, she checked her leave balance on the office system: fourteen days.

The specialist in Singapore said Xin might need a small procedure on her shoulder, and that they would know after one more scan. Before the scan, Xin opened her laptop at the kitchen table and did the practical part in order.
First, she downloaded her company's health insurance policy and searched it for three things: which procedures were covered, whether there was a waiting period for new employees, and how much she would have to pay herself. She had joined seven months ago. The waiting period for planned procedures was six months, so she was just past it. She highlighted that line.
Second, she emailed Olga in HR: 'If I need a procedure, how does medical leave work, and do I need a doctor's letter?' Olga replied the next morning: fourteen days of paid medical leave a year, with a certificate.
Third, she wrote it all on one page and put it in her folder with the scan appointment. Whatever the result, there would be fewer surprises.

qa.q: How long ago had Xin joined the company?
qa.a: Xin joined seven months ago.

qa.q: How might Xin feel after finishing the one-page summary?
qa.a: Calmer and more prepared, less worried about money surprises whatever the scan shows.

qa.q: What else could Xin check with the insurer?
qa.a: Whether the hospital she would use is in their network, and how to get approval before any procedure.

qa.q: How does the request look to Olga in HR?
qa.a: Olga gets a clear, early question that is easy to answer, which helps HR plan any leave too.

grounding: Shows a young worker reading the insurance policy for waiting periods and cover, and asking HR about medical leave before treatment.

subtype: Approach: check the health insurance and work leave rules [Action]
passage:
Charu's doctor had said the next step for her recurring stomach trouble might be a day-care procedure, and her mind went straight to money. The next morning, before starting work at the textile firm in Coimbatore, she went to the HR office on the ground floor.
Raghav, the HR executive, pulled up the group health policy on his screen and turned it toward her. They read it together. Day-care procedures were covered. But she had joined only three months ago, and the policy had a waiting period for planned procedures for new joiners.
'So if I do it now, it's not covered?' Charu asked.
'Not under this. Unless the doctor says it can't wait; then there's an emergency clause.' He printed the page.
Then she asked about leave. Twelve days of sick leave a year, and she had used one.
That evening Charu took the printout back to her doctor, to ask whether it was urgent or could be planned for later.

qa.q: How long ago had Charu joined?
qa.a: Only three months ago.

qa.q: What was Charu worried about after the doctor's visit?
qa.a: She was anxious about the cost of a procedure and whether her insurance would help.

qa.q: Why was taking the printout back to the doctor a good step?
qa.a: It lets the doctor weigh the medical urgency alongside the insurance facts, so any timing decision is made with both in view.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Charu's visit?
qa.a: Raghav sees an employee checking early, and can help her understand the policy before any surprise bill.

grounding: Shows a young worker reading the health policy with HR, finding a waiting period and checking leave rules before planning treatment.
